items.title: Rich Hickey argues LLMs are automation not tools, but others say using AI well requires skill and human judgment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Rich Hickey contends that large language models (LLMs) function as automation rather than tools because they cannot be directly wielded by humans. However, others argue that LLMs can be wielded with skill, requiring users to direct, interpret, and correct outputs much like traditional tools. They emphasize that unpredictability does not disqualify LLMs as tools, and that automation can be a feature within tools, citing examples like compilers and spreadsheets. The debate also touches on the importance of human intention and expertise in using LLMs effectively, with users engaging in feedback loops to refine outputs. Concerns about AI anthropomorphizing and the potential to avoid intellectual work are addressed, highlighting that the key distinction lies in whether users wield AI with understanding and oversight or delegate tasks without adequate control. This perspective suggests a more practical approach to AI as a tool rather than dismissing it outright as automation.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate AI models can embed hidden capabilities via encrypted backdoors resistant to elicitation and interpretation [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have shown that AI models can embed hidden capabilities using encrypted neural networks activated only by secret triggers, making these capabilities provably difficult to detect or interpret even with full access to model weights. They implemented these backdoor attacks in PyTorch and tested their resistance to various elicitation methods on a chemical reaction prediction task, highlighting limitations in current capability evaluation approaches. This work raises concerns about the reliability of audits designed to detect dangerous model behaviors before deployment and underscores the need for improved defenses against such hidden functionalities.

items.title: Meta launches Muse Wonder series, advanced AI models for personal and professional agentic tasks with Active Memory and Active Focus [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta has introduced the Muse Wonder series, including Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, its most capable AI models designed to enhance personal and professional agentic tasks. These models integrate Active Memory and Active Focus to track important information and persistently work toward user goals, marking a significant step toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder is available via the Meta Model API and Muse Code, with Muse Wonder Full accessible to Muse Code subscribers, and will soon power new experiences in Meta's Muse platform.

items.title: Z.ai publishes GLM-Legal blog post on October 12, 2026
items.content_text: Z.ai released a blog post titled GLM-Legal on October 12, 2026, discussing legal aspects related to GLM technology. The post has generated significant discussion on Hacker News, indicating community interest in the topic.

items.title: Intel launches D270 GPU AI accelerator with up to 480 GB LPDDR5X memory for inference-optimized data center workloads [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Intel has introduced the D270 GPU, designed specifically for AI inference in data centers, offering up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X memory and 32 Xe3P cores to support agentic AI workloads. The GPU targets long-context, high-concurrency AI applications, emphasizing power efficiency and compatibility with standard PCIe 5.0 infrastructure. The D270 GPU aims to handle larger AI model contexts and more concurrent sessions without requiring high bandwidth memory or liquid cooling, making it suitable for enterprise AI, SaaS, and sovereign cloud deployments. It supports popular AI frameworks like PyTorch and vLLM, focusing on efficient token serving and scalable inference within existing data center power and rack constraints.

items.title: Agent37 launches low-cost agent sandboxes with free plan enabled by optimized CPU/RAM use and non-hyperscaler hosting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Agent37, a startup founded by a former Amazon engineer, has launched low-cost sandboxes for running AI agents, offering a free plan made possible by infrastructure optimizations. The company reduces costs by managing CPU and RAM usage patterns specific to agent workloads, avoiding hyperscaler cloud providers in favor of vendors like Hetzner and OVH, and using gVisor technology to share resources efficiently across hosts. The free sandboxes cost approximately $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month, enabling over 90% of new signups to use the free tier for hosting personal AI agent code such as Hermes, Openclaw, and Claude. Agent37 targets developers building messaging agents and aims to provide a cost-effective platform tailored to the niche requirements of agent harness workloads.

items.title: Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI predictions foresee Google shifting from search to AI dominance by 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Kevin Kelly's 2016 book The Inevitable predicted that by 2026, Google's main product would shift from search to AI, driven by advances in cloud-based AI and deep learning. Kelly highlighted Google's strategy of using search data to train its AI systems, suggesting that search serves as a means to improve AI rather than the other way around. The predictions also anticipated an oligopoly of a few large cloud-based AI providers and the rise of specialized AI software.

items.title: Character.ai files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy to pursue court-supervised sale amid legal and operational challenges [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Character.ai has initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process to enable a court-supervised sale of the company, aiming to maximize value for stakeholders while continuing platform operations. The company cited significant legal, regulatory, and operational difficulties over the past year as reasons for this decision. The Character.ai platform remains active and accessible, with subscriptions continuing unchanged for now. The sale process is expected to conclude by late November or early December 2026, and the company hopes to find a buyer that will allow the platform to continue operating; otherwise, it will be wound down. User data protections and privacy policies remain in place during this process.

items.title: Linus Torvalds uses AI to improve code readability and uncover bugs in assoc_array library dating back to 2013 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Linus Torvalds applied large language model (LLM) tools to clarify obscure code in the assoc_array library, making it more readable by splitting complex functions. This AI-assisted approach not only confirmed a reported bug but also identified three additional bugs originating from the library's initial 2013 commit. Torvalds' use of AI aligns with his emphasis on clear and maintainable programming practices.

items.title: Researchers outline structural misalignments in Explainable AI faithfulness metrics for feature importance and propose research directions to improve their reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This position paper examines the limitations of current faithfulness metrics used in Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to measure how well explanations align with machine learning models. The authors identify five major shortcomings that hinder rigorous quantification of faithfulness, which affects the trustworthiness of XAI methods often used more as debugging tools than for building user trust. The paper discusses how oversimplification in XAI explanations leads to misalignment with the underlying models, causing unfaithfulness or infidelity. It proposes four research avenues aimed at addressing these challenges to enhance the reliability and computational feasibility of faithfulness metrics in feature importance explanations.

items.title: EliteTable uses large language models to guide self-improving program search for control policies, showing performance gains across six Gymnasium tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: EliteTable is a program-search algorithm that leverages large language models and a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to generate, edit, and remix candidate programs for control tasks. It was tested on six Gymnasium control environments with multiple generations and candidate slots, showing median score improvements in most tasks and transfer of gains to new episodes in some cases. While CartPole-v1 reached peak scores early, other tasks like BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without hitting targets, and Acrobot-v1 showed mixed results. Further comparisons and ablation studies are needed to clarify EliteTable's relative effectiveness and component contributions.

items.title: Controlled study finds Monte Carlo Tree Search 2.88% less effective than randomized-restart list scheduling for DAG workflow scheduling under equal computational budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers conducted a controlled computational study comparing Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and randomized-restart list scheduling for directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflow scheduling, ensuring both methods used the same number of candidate schedule evaluations. The study found that at a budget of 2048 schedules, MCTS performed 2.88% worse than the randomized restarts, with results validated by an independent checker across 768 schedules. The deficit was not due to insufficient budget, and performance varied by workflow structure, with restarts outperforming on sparse irregular workflows and no significant difference on regular or dense workflows. The study was limited to synthetic domains with up to 32 tasks and 8 processors, and results may not generalize to larger budgets or real-world scenarios.

items.title: Researchers propose EvoSyn, a multi-agent framework for agentic data synthesis that adapts and expands generation space using learner feedback to improve task success in interactive AI agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce EvoSyn, a multi-agent system designed to enhance synthetic data generation for interactive agents by using learner feedback to adapt and expand the synthesis space. This framework organizes synthesis around a revisable state that specifies interaction factors and allocates synthesis effort, enabling targeted improvements and discovery of new controllable factors. EvoSyn employs specialized agents to translate feedback into synthesis revisions, with a Designer directing synthesis and a Planner executing experience generation. Experiments on $\tau^2$-Bench and CAR-Bench demonstrate that EvoSyn improves average task success by 13.3 points over leading baselines while producing higher-quality and more structurally diverse synthetic experiences, addressing limitations in existing methods that struggle to close the feedback-to-decision gap in data synthesis for learning agents.

items.title: SpireBench evaluates long-horizon strategic play of 20 large language models in Slay the Spire, showing models match average humans but lag behind experts over extended runs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce SpireBench, a benchmark where large language models play the full commercial deck-building game Slay the Spire to assess long-term strategic reasoning. Testing 20 models at the game's highest difficulty reveals that while frontier models outperform heuristic baselines and match average human players, they fall behind expert players as game runs lengthen, particularly due to misjudging risk and health management during fights. The study finds that models rely partly on prior knowledge of the game and do not improve from in-game memories, which tend to be inaccurate and overly cautious. SpireBench is the first benchmark to provide models with the complete original game and offers tools to analyze where and why agentic models fail in long-horizon tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce Behavioral Self-Rewarding to refine reinforcement learning rewards for software engineering agents, improving debugging quality without new environment interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR), a method that enhances reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards by enabling software engineering agents to judge and compare their own debugging trajectories. BSR refines binary pass/fail rewards into bounded auxiliary rewards based on pairwise preferences, providing additional supervision from existing data without requiring new environment interactions. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench-Live demonstrate consistent performance improvements using Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B models, supporting the use of the policy's own comparative judgments as a complementary learning signal for training software engineering agents.

items.title: Researchers introduce CLEAT, a co-training framework for interactive agents that learns value-guided clarification to improve task performance across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present CLEAT (CLarification through valuE-guided Agent co-Training), a framework that co-trains a clarification-value controller and task policy to help large language model agents ask useful questions and make better decisions when user goals are unstated. CLEAT measures the utility of clarification through paired rollouts and adapts its guidance as the agent learns, achieving top scores on ten evaluation settings across four benchmarks with the Qwen3-4B model. CLEAT improves task policy performance even without the controller at inference and shows significant gains over strong baselines, including 13.2 and 6.5 percentage points improvements on UserGym Travel and IN3 underspecification judgment accuracy, respectively. The approach addresses the challenge of interactive intent alignment by enabling agents to effectively use clarifications to handle incomplete information and evolving policies.

items.title: Researchers introduce MagicBeanStalk, a recursive data synthesis algorithm that generates policy- and budget-calibrated training problems to overcome the zero-advantage trap in RLVR datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers identify that a large open-source math corpus used in reinforcement learning with verifiable reasoning (RLVR) largely falls into a zero-advantage trap, where most problems are either always solved or always failed for a fixed policy and rollout budget. To address this, they develop MagicBeanStalk, an algorithm that recursively synthesizes new training problems calibrated to the target policy and training budget, preserving the reasoning structure of seed problems. Testing across eight math benchmarks, continual RLVR training on MagicBeanStalk-generated problems improves model performance significantly more than training on the full original corpus or its filtered subsets. The approach also synthesizes over 14,000 verifiable finance problems from 340 solutions, yielding notable accuracy gains on finance benchmarks SecQue and FinanceBench.

items.title: Researchers develop LLM-driven pipeline to automate construction of hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs from datasheets, achieving 98.8% property faithfulness across diverse components [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present an automated pipeline using large language models (LLMs) to convert hardware datasheets into hierarchical knowledge graphs that organize engineering specifications for component selection and system integration. The approach uses chunk-based extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement to preserve source provenance and reduce context size, improving accuracy over one-shot methods. The framework was evaluated on 20 hardware datasheets covering various component types and lengths, achieving 98.8% property faithfulness compared to 76.1% for a baseline method and covering 83.6% of baseline properties fully. These knowledge graphs provide more reliable and comprehensive engineering data to support hardware design and verification, reducing risks of overlooked constraints and errors.

items.title: Researchers propose distilled optimal transport method to align pretrained unimodal encoders using 100-500 paired examples amid abundant unpaired data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a method that aligns two independently pretrained unimodal encoders with only 100 to 500 paired examples, leveraging abundant unpaired data on either side. Their approach represents each data point by its similarity to paired anchors, aligns the modalities via an entropic optimal transport problem with marginal constraints to mitigate hubness, and distills the alignment into lightweight encoders for inductive correspondence. The method requires pairing only for anchor points, allowing unpaired data to be drawn independently from each modality's distribution. Evaluations on image-text and molecule-text alignment tasks demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods on datasets including Flickr30k, MS-COCO, and ChEBI-20 at comparable anchor budgets.

items.title: Researchers introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model for LLM agents that updates environment knowledge through falsifiable hypotheses to improve task performance across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: EvoBelief is a new approach for large language model (LLM) agents that evolves their beliefs about environment dynamics during deployment by forming and validating falsifiable hypotheses. Unlike traditional methods that update model parameters, EvoBelief maintains a frozen language model and updates rules linked to evidence, allowing agents to adapt to changes and improve predictions and planning. The system was tested on four benchmarks including ALFWorld, MiniGrid, and DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, showing significant improvements in success rates and the ability to revise stale rules and discover quantitative laws. EvoBelief demonstrated up to 31.3% higher success than comparable frozen models and completed tasks that baseline methods could not, highlighting its potential for self-improvement through testable and revisable environment knowledge.

items.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.

items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.

items.title: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks routinely develop representations in which individual neurons contribute to multiple distinct functions, leading to the widespread view that such networks lack modular organization. We challenge this conclusion by introducing a formally nested hierarchy of modularity: unit-level, which requires distinct computations to occupy disjoint neurons; orthogonal, which asks whether a rotation reveals functionally independent subspaces; and linear, which asks whether a bounded linear map can separate task-relevant computations into independent subspaces. We develop a unified framework for learning decompositions at each level and evaluating them causally through selective ablation. Across vision models, language models and multi-task Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), we find that networks which lack unit-level modularity nonetheless often exhibit clear functional modularity at the subspace level. In vision and language models, content versus style and syntax versus semantics respectively dissociate under subspace ablation despite sharing overlapping populations of neurons. These learned subspaces also align differentially with brain data, with content and style subspaces predicting higher and lower visual cortex respectively, and semantic subspaces outperforming syntactic ones in predicting language cortex activity. In RNNs trained on multiple cognitive tasks and previously shown to lack modular structure, our decomposition recovers sharp double dissociations between tasks. The absence of unit-level modularity frequently coexists with clear subspace-level modularity across domains, enabling targeted intervention on specific computations even in networks where no individual neuron is specialized, with broad implications for mechanistic interpretability and for understanding functional organization in both biological and artificial neural systems.

items.title: Towards Defining, Measuring, and Leveraging Creativity in AI Applications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite extensive research, computational creativity still lacks a conceptually grounded, practically relevant, and empirically applicable formal definition across contexts such as art, scientific research, and games. Existing approaches to creativity often focus on proposing informal conceptual definitions without providing formal computational concepts. Alternatively, they propose formal definitions without carefully examining their underlying assumptions or providing validation of these definitions by testing their performance in specific application settings. To address these problems, this paper proposes several formal postulates of creativity grounded in prior psychological work on creativity, especially as related to Boden's three core criteria of creativity: newness, value, and surprise. Furthermore, we propose a conceptual mathematical definition of creativity that aligns with these postulates. We also validate our proposed creativity formula in two applications: determining the creativity of particular chess moves, and assessing the creativity of paintings by some artists, such as Picasso, Renoir, and other painters. Experimental results demonstrate that our formula of creativity successfully captures creative patterns across both the chess and the art domains. This suggests that creativity can be effectively characterized through a unified mathematical structure based on three fundamental criteria, namely newness, value, and surprise, whose specific measurements are adapted to the particular domains.

items.title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. However, we find that OPSD methods can progressively degrade previously acquired capabilities: queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages may become incorrectly responded as optimization proceeds, even the overall performance continues to improve. Further analysis reveals that this degradation coincides with a deterioration of the geometry of hidden representations, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and diminished inter-cluster separation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which preserves representation geometry during post-training by encouraging compactness within cluster and separation across cluster. RGR can be seamlessly integrated into existing OPSD methods without altering their core optimization procedures. Extensive experiments on multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show that RGR generally alleviates capability degradation while retaining capability improvements. Our code is available in https://github.com/supermachinelearner/RGR.

items.title: Collaborative Theory of Mind: Learning to Self-Revise by Anticipating User Responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong individual task performance, yet still struggle to collaborate with users over extended, multi-turn interactions, for example by attempting solutions before understanding the user's needs or by failing to revise mistaken assumptions after receiving feedback. We propose Collaborative Theory of Mind (CToM), a framework that addresses these challenges by explicitly training LLMs to anticipate user responses and to use those predictions to improve their own behavior. CToM drafts a response, predicts how the user will respond, and uses this prediction to guide internal revision before presenting a response. During training, the user's reply to each draft serves as the target for predicting the next turn, and we train the assistant to minimize the negative log-likelihood of that reply. We combine this prediction objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to optimize both task performance and interaction efficiency. Across mathematical reasoning, coding, and writing tasks, CToM achieves higher collaborative task performance than all baselines; for example, on a collaborative mathematical reasoning task, it improves final accuracy from 74.1% to 79.6% compared with naive GRPO. Ablations show that predicting user responses also makes collaboration more efficient: under the same reward, adding prediction supervision reduces the number of user replies by 8% on coding and 17% on writing while improving task performance. Behavioral analyses of interaction trajectories show that user-response predictions become more accurate after training, and that more accurate predictions are associated with larger improvements in collaborative task performance through self-revision.

items.title: One-Step Text Generation by Seq-Drifting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but still require multiple sampling steps to produce high-quality text. In this paper, we investigate whether a model can learn to generate an entire sequence in a single forward pass. We propose Seq-Drifting, a framework that applies drifting to sequences of continuous token representations and directly learns a map from Gaussian noise to text. Unlike existing DLMs that derive the supervision at each position directly from the observed token in a training sequence, Seq-Drifting builds a drift field whose position-wise targets adapt to the current generated context. At each position, attraction guides each output toward a set of contextually plausible token representations, while repulsion discourages collapse across samples and repetition within sequences. The generator learns from this drift field during training and produces all tokens jointly in one pass at inference. Empirically, Seq-Drifting achieves a generative perplexity of 36.01 on LM1B in one step and performs competitively in both unconditional and conditional generation. Experiments on translation, summarization, and reasoning further demonstrate the applicability of the framework beyond open-ended generation. These results suggest that drifting over token sequences offers a promising path toward effective one-step text generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/jyliu-ai/Seq-Drifting.

items.title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.

items.title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.

items.title: DeFiRank: Federated Pairwise Ranking for Governance in Decentralized Financial Networks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing governance approaches in decentralized financial networks rely on manual review processes conducted by human committees, which introduces subjective bias, creates a scalability bottleneck under high network volume, and fails to capture complex behavioural patterns and evolving network dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose \name, a federated learning-based pairwise ranking framework in which multiple institutions collaboratively train a ranking model without sharing their private transaction data. This collaborative learning enables the model to capture network-wide behavioural patterns that signify strong network participation and directly contribute to the network effect, including diversity of counterparties, usage of multiple applications, and frequency of transactions. The proposed system ranks providers based on the authenticity of their actions, promoting genuine contributors and demoting those exhibiting suspicious behaviour. We evaluate \name\ on a real-world blockchain transaction dataset. Results demonstrate that the federated approach achieves ranking performance modestly below the centralized baseline (NDCG@15: $\approx$0.87 vs.\ $\approx$0.92) while preserving data privacy and matching its ranking stability (Kendall $\tau$: $\approx$0.70 for both regimes), producing reliable governance decisions, including provider promotion and demotion (648 and 39 unique providers, respectively), without requiring centralized access to sensitive transaction data.

items.title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI shopping assistants increasingly influence which products consumers consider. We study retail assortment planning under AI mediation, where a retailer chooses a catalog, an AI intermediary forms a customer-facing shortlist, and the customer chooses from that shortlist according to a multinomial logit model. We consider both deterministic mediation, in which the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation based on the Plackett-Luce model. Empirically, we construct a dataset of product rankings from leading AI models, estimate Plackett-Luce ranking models, and evaluate their predictive performance on held-out assortments. Combining these estimates with synthetic customer preferences, we find that accounting for AI mediation can materially change optimal assortments and revenue. Across the tested capacity configurations, ignoring mediation yields mean revenue losses between 2.52% and 11.37% relative to the PL optimum. A much simpler deterministic plug-in, based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities, performs substantially better, with mean losses of at most 0.53%. Motivated by this performance, we study assortment optimization under deterministic mediation. We characterize its computational complexity and show that, for any fixed number of customer segments, the problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

items.title: Teaching neural decoders with language [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces decode neural activity, yet class-label supervision (CLS) leaves relationships among classes implicit. We propose Language as Supervision (LaS), which aligns neural features with natural-language class descriptions through learned projections and predicts classes using candidate text prototypes. We evaluate seven encoder architectures with independently trained models for visual, motor, and speech decoding from scalp and intracranial recordings. LaS improves speech-decoding accuracy by up to 17.15~pp over matched CLS baselines. Its representations support candidate-set reuse and label-supervised subject and session adaptation, while LaS enables conditional unseen-frequency decoding in steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) responses. Correct class-description correspondence supports this generalization, and dual-sided attribution visualization shows neural and textual contributions to the same class-matching score. These findings suggest that text descriptions can serve as general-purpose references for learning and interpretation in neural decoding.

items.title: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks, benefiting from knowledge priors, in-context reasoning, and test-time computation. Despite these strengths, single-model reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, as later steps depend on the model's earlier outputs, leaving reasoning blind spots difficult to independently reassess. To address this limitation, we develop \textit{collaborative learning}, encompassing the construction of heterogeneous collaborators and the learning of effective cross-model collaboration. Specifically, \textit{model slicing} replaces a large model with smaller, heterogeneous models under a comparable parameter budget, enabling prior reasoning to be reassessed across distinct model parameterizations. \textit{Pyramid supervision} combines protocol distillation with step-level supervision to refine reasoning and interaction decisions throughout collaboration. We evaluate our approach across four task categories: multi-hop question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended constrained generation. The trained heterogeneous models achieve comparable or better task performance than the original large model and established multi-agent baselines, including reinforcement-learning-based methods, while also achieving higher inference efficiency than the multi-agent baselines and exhibiting differentiated collaboration patterns across tasks. These findings show that learned collaboration turns model heterogeneity into complementary reasoning capabilities.

items.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

items.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.

items.title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).

items.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Finite-Beam Reachability and Continuous-Query Generation in Generative Recommendation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) of social media platforms commonly retrieves items by autoregressively decoding discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) with finite-width beam search. This work examines how this output interface constrains whether held-out targets enter finite returned lists, while distinguishing catalog-wide scoreability from empirical top-K support. We introduce two continuous-query paradigms: CQG-Single generates one retrieval query in a single pass, and CQG-AR autoregressively generates continuous residual updates, retaining step-wise decoding while removing the SID item-token vocabulary, code lookup, and discrete beam expansion. These designs thereby eliminate the SID-specific reachability constraint induced by finite-beam decoding and avoid the technical challenge of aligning a discrete SID vocabulary with the pretrained backbone's vector space. Both methods make every encoded item directly scoreable through dense or approximate-nearest-neighbor retrieval. Under a unified protocol with valid-prefix constrained decoding, CQG-Single exceeds the TIGER-style baseline in all seven runs while using 55.3% as many trainable parameters. CQG-AR remains comparable on ML-1M and is numerically stronger on Beauty and Sports datasets. A controlled depth ablation further shows that additional continuous refinement does not monotonically improve shallow accuracy. These findings motivate decoupling output representation, autoregressive modeling, and retrieval budget when evaluating generative recommendation systems.

items.title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.

items.title: Benchmarking Embedding Geometries and Clustering Algorithms for Unsupervised Patent Claim Classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.12997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior-art retrieval systems are structurally organized around classification codes, making cross-code discovery difficult. This paper asks if an unsupervised representation trained on patent text can recover relevant connections that code-restricted search cannot, and if hyperbolic space helps. We trained a hyperbolic and a matched Euclidean Variational Autoencoder (VAE) on 45,000 US patents (96 runs, 6 seeds). The hyperbolic model retrieves genuinely cross-category prior art 52% more often than the Euclidean model (18.76% vs. 12.34% of top-10 results, 3,000 queries). This represents a practical gain for the motivating search problem. The hyperbolic model agrees less with official classification (NMI 0.2392 vs. 0.3206), which we explain geometrically: the two measures capture different goals, and only one aligns with prior-art search needs. In a study of 10 technology domains (50,000 more patents), we find that a domain's classification breadth--the number of distinct CPC subgroups spanned--predicts approach performance (Pearson r=-0.642, p=0.045, N=10), and that patents per subgroup is an even stronger predictor (r=0.715, p=0.020). This provides a checkable signal for practitioners to determine where the method is most valuable. We report all findings with statistical transparency and release a complete, 91-test automated implementation.

items.title: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.

items.title: Scaling Empowered Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.

items.title: Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.

items.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.

items.title: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State-Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch-advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration. Experiments across four interactive benchmark MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind primitive provides limited benefit and can even degrade performance. In contrast, ReTRAIL enables agents to rewind from unproductive states and use insights from abandoned branches to guide subsequent exploration. These results demonstrate the value of coupling environment rewinding with experience reuse within an ongoing task for long-horizon task solving. The code is available at https://github.com/whi497/ReTRAIL.

items.title: LongHarness: Advancing Agentic Reasoning over 100M-Token Corpora via Stateful Evidence Management [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.

items.title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.

items.title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.

items.title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.

items.title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.

items.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.

items.title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) acquire advanced biological design capabilities, they offer substantial research benefits but simultaneously introduce severe dual-use risks, such as engineering enhanced pathogens or drug-resistant bacteria. While biosecurity frameworks recognize these threats, the actual risk of LLMs executing dangerous biological modifications remains unquantified, particularly when augmented with specialized biological design tools (BDTs). Existing evaluations primarily assess hazardous knowledge possession rather than practical application, overlook risk amplification from BDTs, and rely on unreliable, expensive, or hazardous validation methods. To address these gaps, we introduce DRYLAB-Bench (Design Risk Yielded by LLM Agent in Biodesign), the first comprehensive benchmark evaluating the high-risk biological mutation design capabilities of LLM agents. Moving beyond basic question-answering, DRYLAB-Bench tasks agents with 30 genuinely hazardous mutation-design scenarios distilled from biosecurity guidelines. It evaluates models in a multi-round, tool-augmented environment where LLMs orchestrate BDTs to iteratively refine candidates. Crucially, it scores designs directly against 187,695 empirical wet-lab measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym using our proposed Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS), quantifying risk-associated effects while enabling scalable and safe ground-truth verification. Evaluations of 15 frontier models reveal substantial baseline threats: without tools, 67.6% of one-shot designs exceed the average measured variant, and 21.4% reach the highest-risk decile. Equipping models with BDTs significantly amplifies this risk, raising the pooled risk by \(\Delta BRS=+0.116\) and the top-decile share to 23.5%. Code: https://github.com/drylab-bio/DRYLAB-Bench

items.title: Locate, Judge, Read: Role-Specialized Tool Agents over a Knowledge-Point Index for Open-Domain Multimodal Document QA [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Question answering over large heterogeneous document collections requires first finding the right passages and then reading them, yet current retrieval-augmented agents give one model both kinds of tools and let it schedule itself. We present KnowForge, a pipeline separated by job: a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index; a Locator agent that can only search; a code-scheduled bridge judge that forces the missing second hop; a typed, size-bounded evidence pool that merges every search's ranking; a Deep Reader agent that can only read text, images and tables; and a synthesizer with a format checker. With a self-hosted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (3B active), KnowForge reaches F1 47.5 on the full open-domain M3DocVQA (2,441 questions, 3,368 PDFs), +11.0 over the published M3DocRAG system and +7.1 over one-shot retrieve-and-answer on the same index and model, and 53.5 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. On MultiHop-RAG it reaches 73.5 accuracy, above the strongest published RAG and GraphRAG results (71.2); on the single-document MMLongBench-Doc it lifts the same model from 34.8 to 47.0, level with GPT-4o reading page images (46.3). Per-job ablations on the full benchmarks attribute the gain: the Deep Reader is worth 3.8, 9.8 and 0 points on the three corpora, tracking how visual each is; merging both agents into one with all tools and twice the rounds loses 1.9 F1 because it keeps searching instead of reading; a round-budget sweep shows a step at four Locator rounds and a plateau beyond; query latency scales with model calls rather than corpus size. We serve the three indexed benchmarks as read-only knowledge bases (free registration) and release all prompts and the runner code: https://github.com/metask-ai/knowforge-bench

items.title: Looking Ahead and Back: Anticipatory Generative Modeling for Road-Network Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trajectory generation underpins urban applications such as traffic management and urban planning. Within road networks, vehicle movement along road segments is largely deterministic, whereas transitions at intersections are critical--multiple outgoing paths may appear equally plausible, yet they can lead to substantially different downstream routes. Existing generative methods such as diffusion models simulate location sequences and fail short of next transition selection, even producing trajectories that drift off the road network. To fill this gap, we advocate a fundamental shift: moving beyond location simulation toward behavior modeling on the road network. In this paper, we revisit trajectory generation through the lens of generative route planning, and introduce a new graph-constrained generative paradigm, Anticipatory Generative Modeling, which resolves next transition selection by incorporating the Anticipation of how the future route may unfold toward the destination. Concretely, we propose a novel generative model named Foresight that formulates a probabilistic model for an "anticipate--select--update--re-anticipate" loop that enables longer-term foresight while continuing sequential generation along the historical trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Foresight wins state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: DP-MIND: Differentially private memory-guided Long context Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation. In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.

items.title: Competence-Aware Orchestration for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning through role specialization and collaboration, yet a key challenge remains: how can collaboration be adapted to a backbone's competence on the current query? This problem matters because more collaboration is not always better--richer coordination may help on difficult cases, but it also incurs additional token cost and redundant interactions. We propose a two-stage competence-aware framework for automatic MAS orchestration. It first models the LLM backbone's task-conditioned competence for the current query, and then uses this signal to adapt role activation and the communication graph. Across six benchmarks, our method achieves an average score of 93.81%. Experiments with six LLM backbones of varying competence levels further show that our method adjusts collaboration according to the inferred competence: for higher-competence backbones, it improves average accuracy from 87.22 to 89.97 while reducing token cost by 36.26%; for lower-competence backbones, it yields a further average gain of 4.58 points over existing methods. The same trend also holds on unseen backbones.

items.title: VIGOR: Verifiable Industrial Geometry Optimization and Repair in Scene Programs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate structured layouts and executable scene programs from natural-language instructions. However, executability does not imply engineering feasibility: an industrial scene program may execute successfully while its final state still violates coupled boundary, collision, clearance, aisle, or structural constraints. We identify this mismatch as the executability-engineering-feasibility gap, where locally plausible placements can remain globally infeasible because corrections to one device may introduce violations elsewhere. To make this gap measurable in a controlled setting, we construct an execution-grounded industrial scene-program dataset with 1,749 constructible scenarios, complete executable programs, and 94 final-state geometric checks per scenario. We further propose VIGOR, which combines supervised scene-program generation with execution-grounded verification and staged geometric refinement. Supervised fine-tuning establishes complete program generation, local projection resolves independently correctable violations, and joint conflict-graph repair coordinates residual multi-object conflicts while preserving structural relations. Experiments show that VIGOR achieves 96.86% Complete Feasibility and an Overall score of 91.20, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.42 points in Overall. These results show that, under controlled industrial layout conditions, reliable scene-program generation requires not only executable programs, but also explicit verification and coordinated resolution of coupled engineering constraints.

items.title: Quality, Not Just Outcome: A Structural Scoring Framework for Selecting Coding-Agent Trajectories for Supervised Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open coding agents are commonly trained through supervised fine-tuning on interaction trajectories whose final patches pass the benchmark test suite. However, this outcome-level filtering criterion ignores process quality: trajectories that eventually succeed may still contain inefficient interaction patterns such as repetitive file inspection, unstable tool usage, or delayed modification behavior, all of which become part of the imitation target. We propose TQS (Trajectory Quality Score), a structural scoring framework for coding-agent trajectories that operates directly on trajectory structure, requires no LLM judge, and runs in linear time. TQS characterizes trajectory quality through structural signals organized around structured convergence: information focus, intent--action alignment, and policy dynamics. Using 155,144 successful trajectories from a public open-license corpus, we rank trajectories by TQS and fine-tune coding agents on filtered subsets. Models trained on top-ranked trajectories consistently outperform those trained on random or bottom-ranked subsets on SWE-Bench-Verified. Our results suggest that process-level trajectory quality is an important factor in coding-agent supervision and that structural trajectory filtering provides an effective and scalable alternative to LLM-based data selection.

items.title: RoleWorld: Knowledge Transfer in World Modeling with Functional Role Abstractions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.13172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models enable large language model (LLM) agents to anticipate action effects and make informed decisions.
